network.overall_strategy: Construct ten operationally distinct routes: four experimentally observed discharge endpoints, one acetone-derived photochemical route, two aldehyde-entry Strecker variants, and three catalyst-specific reductive aminations of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate. These are not ten independently demonstrated end-to-end prebiotic mechanisms. The unresolved synthesis of alpha-ketoisocaproate is not replaced by an invented reaction. P5-P7 extend aminonitrile chemistry using an explicitly specified forcing acid-hydrolysis benchmark; their completion under naturally occurring conditions remains unvalidated. P8-P10 begin with an explicitly declared ketoacid inventory and do not receive material from the sulfidic photochemical branch. Discharge nodes summarize experimentally observed production and analytical workup, not elementary reactions or complete product-mixture balances. Their environment denotes the primary formation setting; separate analytical hydrolysis is identified explicitly. All net reaction channels conserve atoms with inferred coefficients. Neutral molecular formulas represent pH-dependent acid/base pools, with counterions omitted. S8 is a formal sulfur oxidation-product sink, not an assertion that only S8 forms. Because the schema lacks a coproduct role, terminal coproducts use the intermediate role. Starting inventories and their geological availability are distinguished from demonstrated transformations. No oxygen, enzymes, stereoselectivity, integrated yield, or independently verified natural implementation is assumed.

reactions.name: Methane-fed discharge: empirical leucine-production and workup module

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk collection apparatus; 383 K only during separate analytical hydrolysis
conditions.pressure: Reported initial dry-gas charge approximately 380 mmHg, before water-vapor contribution
conditions.catalyst: No discharge catalyst; hydronium catalyzes the analytical hydrolysis
conditions.other: Anoxic electrical discharge over an aqueous collector. Reported methane-run composition: 300 torr CH4, 80 torr N2, 0.1 torr NH3, and 0.05 M NH4Cl at pH 8.7. N2 is part of the gas atmosphere; the net channel uses the supplied ammonia reservoir as its nitrogen source. A 72 h discharge is a proposed comparison protocol, not a duration verified from the supplied Ring report. For an explicitly defined total-amino-acid endpoint, use the separate 6 M HCl, 383 K, 24 h analytical benchmark described in rxn_009.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical discharge generates a complex reactive mixture, including cyanide and carbonyl precursors. Aqueous capture and Strecker-type chemistry contribute amino-acid precursors, with analytical hydrolysis releasing additional leucine. The net channel is balanceable as 6 methane + ammonia + 2 water -> leucine + 9 hydrogen; it is not an elementary mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Leucine production from methane-containing discharge mixtures is directly supported by Ring et al. (1972) and Ring and Miller (1984). Reported Leu/Gly ratios are approximately 0.014-0.076, with poor discrimination against other C6 amino-acid isomers. The precise leucine-forming intermediates and free-versus-hydrolysable fractions are not fully resolved. Hydrogen is a permissible balancing coproduct, not a reported leucine-correlated yield. The discharge setting requires locally reducing gases, and analytical acid hydrolysis must not be mistaken for demonstrated natural processing.

reactions.name: Isobutane-fed discharge: empirical branched-hydrocarbon route

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk collection apparatus; 383 K only during separate analytical hydrolysis
conditions.pressure: 0.5-1 bar total gas pressure as a proposed comparison window
conditions.catalyst: No discharge catalyst; hydronium catalyzes the analytical hydrolysis
conditions.other: Anoxic isobutane-containing discharge atmosphere and aqueous ammonia collector. Proposed comparison conditions: pH 8-9, 0.05-0.15 M total ammonia, and 72 h discharge. Exact isobutane-run partial pressures and duration are not supplied in the research summary and are not asserted here. Analyze the hydrolysable endpoint using 6 M HCl at 383 K for 24 h, separately from the discharge stage.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge fragmentation and recombination generate a mixed carbonyl/cyanide inventory from a branched hydrocarbon feed. Subsequent aqueous precursor formation and hydrolysis yield leucine among many products. The represented channel balances as 3 isobutane + 2 ammonia + 4 water -> 2 leucine + 9 hydrogen.
reactions.reasoning: Ring and Miller (1984) reported leucine at approximately 6.7 per 100 glycine for an isobutane feed. This supports the empirical endpoint, not a selective conversion of an intact isobutane skeleton into leucine. The proposed operating window is a comparison design rather than a reconstructed published protocol. Geological availability of sufficient isobutane, broad product distributions, and dependence on analytical hydrolysis remain limitations.

reactions.name: Acetylene-fed discharge: empirical unsaturated-carbon route

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk collection apparatus; 383 K only during separate analytical hydrolysis
conditions.pressure: 0.5-1 bar total gas pressure as a proposed comparison window
conditions.catalyst: No discharge catalyst; hydronium catalyzes the analytical hydrolysis
conditions.other: Anoxic acetylene-containing electrical discharge with aqueous collection. Proposed comparison conditions: pH 8-9, 0.05-0.15 M total ammonia, and 72 h discharge. Exact original acetylene-run gas composition and residence time are not available in the supplied summary. Separate endpoint hydrolysis: 6 M HCl, 383 K, 24 h.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-driven carbon-chain growth produces a complex mixture of amino-acid precursors. The empirical leucine channel balances as 3 acetylene + ammonia + 2 water -> leucine. This equation describes one product channel, not selective gas conversion.
reactions.reasoning: Ring and Miller (1984) reported approximately 14 leucine per 100 glycine with acetylene feed. This is a demonstrated feedstock-dependent endpoint rather than evidence for a resolved acetylene-to-isovaleraldehyde mechanism. Absolute selectivity remains low, and the availability of concentrated acetylene and ammonia is a local-geochemistry constraint.

reactions.name: Sulfidic volcanic discharge: empirical leucine-production module

conditions.temperature: Approximately 373 K boiling-water reservoir with cooler collection zones; 383 K only for the selected analytical hydrolysis benchmark
conditions.pressure: Reported initial gas partial pressures: CH4 258, H2S 100, NH3 250, and CO2 87 mmHg
conditions.catalyst: No mineral catalyst; hydronium catalyzes the analytical hydrolysis
conditions.other: Reported experiment: 300 mL water and 3 days of electrical discharge. Collector pH was not provided in the supplied summary; pH 7-9 is a proposed monitoring window, not a reported measurement. H2S participates in radical chemistry and is not assumed to be an indefinitely regenerated catalyst. The explicitly selected analytical endpoint uses 6 M HCl at 383 K for 24 h, not a claimed reproduction of the archived-sample workup.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge chemistry involving sulfide-derived radicals promotes alkyl-radical and carbonyl formation, followed by mixed aqueous amino-acid-precursor chemistry. One atom-balanced formal channel is 11 methane + carbon dioxide + 2 ammonia + 8 hydrogen sulfide + 2 water -> 2 leucine + 22 hydrogen + S8.
reactions.reasoning: Parker et al. (2011, PNAS) detected leucine in the archived H2S-rich experiment; Parker et al. (2011, Origins of Life and Evolution of Biospheres) discussed alkyl-radical enhancement. The encoded equation is an endpoint bookkeeping channel, not an experimentally measured sulfur or hydrogen balance. Actual sulfur products are heterogeneous. The reducing gas composition was not necessarily globally representative, and neither leucine-specific high yield nor natural completion of the analytical hydrolysis is established.

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Proposed test conditions: acetone 10-50 mM, total HCN/CN 10-100 mM, pH 8-9, and 1-24 h equilibration. These concentrations and times are design brackets, not a leucine-specific optimized protocol from the supplied literature. Exclude added ammonia until the intended aminonitrile-forming stage. Limit loss of volatile feedstocks.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to acetone followed by proton transfer forms the cyanohydrin. Subsequent consumption by photoreduction can pull this otherwise incomplete equilibrium forward.
reactions.reasoning: Acetone cyanohydrin is an intermediate in the leucine-related cyanosulfidic sequence of Patel et al. (2015), reviewed by Green, Xu and Sutherland (2021). The reaction does not require an added mineral catalyst. Acetone is a declared starting inventory; no unverified upstream C1-to-acetone synthesis is inserted. Concentration, volatility, and competing cyanide chemistry remain environmental constraints.

reactions.name: First staged photoreductive homologation to isobutyraldehyde cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous, phosphate-buffered, staged irradiation at 254 nm. Proposed screening brackets: pH 7-8, organic substrate approximately 10 mM, total cyanide 10-50 mM, total sulfide 20-100 mM, and copper 0.1-1 mM. Irradiate individual stages for 1-24 h while monitoring conversion; this is a proposed test window, not a verified integrated leucine protocol. Sulfide/cyanide replenishment and condition changes may be required.

reactions.mechanism: A coarse-grained sequence of sulfur-assisted nitrile reduction, deoxygenation, aldehyde formation and cyanide recapture homologates the carbon skeleton. Transient thioamide-related species are included within the module rather than represented as one elementary transformation. Formal redox bookkeeping consumes two H2S per homologation and produces ammonia plus oxidized sulfur.
reactions.reasoning: The staged acetone-derived homologation is supported by Patel et al. (2015) and Green, Xu and Sutherland (2021). Copper is justified by its photoredox role, not merely its presence in minerals. S8 represents an aggregate sulfur oxidation sink. The stated screening conditions require experimental verification for this module. Sulfide availability, UV attenuation, realistic irradiation times and sequential handling are limitations identified by Ranjan et al. (2018) and Rimmer et al. (2021).

reactions.name: Second staged photoreductive homologation to the leucine cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Continue only after establishing the preceding carbon-skeleton transformation. Use staged 254 nm irradiation under anoxia. Proposed screening brackets: pH 7-8, approximately 10 mM organic substrate, 10-50 mM total cyanide, 20-100 mM total sulfide, and 0.1-1 mM copper. Monitor each 1-24 h irradiation stage rather than assuming completion from elapsed time. Delay deliberate ammonia enrichment, which would divert the preceding cyanohydrin toward the valine aminonitrile.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfur-assisted reduction and deoxygenation generate the isovaleraldehyde-level skeleton, followed by cyanide addition to give 2-hydroxy-4-methylpentanenitrile. The multistage module has the same formal two-H2S reducing requirement per homologation as rxn_006.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) and Green, Xu and Sutherland (2021) describe the further homologation leading to the leucine aminonitrile precursor. This module captures that stepwise chemistry without claiming a single-pot elementary process. No full acetone-to-leucine yield is available in the supplied evidence. Sequential reagent management and suppression of competing branches are important bottlenecks; the numerical screening window is proposed rather than experimentally validated as an integrated sequence.

reactions.name: Ammonia-mediated conversion of the leucine cyanohydrin to aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed test conditions: cyanohydrin 10-50 mM, total ammonia 0.1-0.5 M, pH 8-9, and 24-72 h with analytical monitoring. Stop photochemical processing before deliberate ammonia enrichment. The chosen ammonia range is a concentration requirement to test, not an established natural pool inventory or a reproduced published leucine-specific protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Coupled cyanohydrin dissociation, aldehyde-ammonia condensation and cyanide capture favor the alpha-aminonitrile. This is not modeled as direct displacement of hydroxide from an unactivated alcohol.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report access to the leucine alpha-aminonitrile upon ammonia addition to the relevant cyanohydrin sequence; Green, Xu and Sutherland (2021) review the branch. The aminonitrile, not free leucine, is the reported endpoint supporting this reaction. Adequate ammonia activity is essential because cyanohydrin persistence and hydroxy-acid formation compete. The proposed residence time and concentrations require verification.

reactions.name: Forcing acid hydrolysis of leucine aminonitrile to leucine

conditions.pressure: Closed aqueous reactor at approximately 1-2 bar autogenous pressure
conditions.other: Explicit laboratory completion benchmark: 6 M HCl, 24 h, anoxic closed batch, UV off. Analyze both residual aminonitrile/amide and recovered leucine; extend residence time only if conversion and survival measurements justify it. Ammonia is present predominantly as ammonium in this medium. These are forcing analytical conditions, not a claimed naturally occurring prebiotic pool. The supplied sources do not validate an isolated leucine-aminonitrile yield under this exact protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed nitrile hydration passes through leucinamide, followed by amide hydrolysis. Both transformations are included explicitly in this net module: one aminonitrile plus two waters gives leucine plus ammonia in the neutral-form convention.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker amino-acid formation by hydrolysis is established chemistry discussed by Miller (1957), and acid-released amino-acid endpoints occur in the discharge literature including Parker et al. (2011). The selected 6 M HCl, 383 K, 24 h treatment is a forcing hydrolysis benchmark, not a protocol attributed verbatim to those papers. Its application to the isolated leucine aminonitrile and to the complete Patel mixture is an inferred extension requiring substrate-specific recovery measurements. It directly avoids assuming rapid mild amide hydrolysis. Geological access to such strongly acidic conditions, crude-mixture compatibility and natural residence times remain unresolved. Aubrey, Cleaves and Bada (2009) caution against assuming amino-acid survival during prolonged hydrothermal exposure.

reactions.name: Direct Strecker aminonitrile formation from supplied isovaleraldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed batch: isovaleraldehyde approximately 10 mM, total cyanide approximately 20 mM, total ammonia 0.1-0.5 M, pH 8-9, and 24-72 h. Use an anoxic, evaporation-limited aqueous collector. These are proposed screening conditions, not a retrieved leucine-specific yield protocol. Subsequent hydrolysis requires the separately specified rxn_009 conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condenses with 3-methylbutanal to form an imine/iminium pool; cyanide addition produces 2-amino-4-methylpentanenitrile and water. The aldehyde supplies the branched C5 unit, and cyanide supplies the future carboxyl carbon.
reactions.reasoning: This is the structurally correct classical Strecker route to leucine, consistent with Miller (1957) and the interpretation of discharge amino-acid synthesis in Ring and Miller (1984). The supplied research does not establish an optimized isolated-substrate protocol under the proposed conditions. Isovaleraldehyde is an explicit external starting inventory, not a claimed selectively synthesized discharge intermediate. Ammonia availability and competing cyanohydrin formation are limiting factors, and environmental completion remains conditional on hydrolysis.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin entry route from supplied isovaleraldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed test conditions: aldehyde 10-50 mM, total cyanide 10-100 mM, pH 8-9, and 1-24 h equilibration. Initially exclude added ammonia to favor cyanohydrin accumulation, then change conditions according to rxn_008. No irradiation is required for this carbonyl-addition step.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to the aldehyde carbonyl gives 2-hydroxy-4-methylpentanenitrile, preserving the isobutyl side-chain connectivity.
reactions.reasoning: Ordinary aldehyde cyanohydrin chemistry supplies the same intermediate used in the leucine branch of Patel et al. (2015). Direct preparation from an externally supplied aldehyde is a chemically justified entry variant, not an independently demonstrated complete prebiotic leucine route in the supplied report. Its later conversion to leucine shares rxn_008 and the hydrolysis limitations of rxn_009.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalyzed reductive amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate

conditions.other: Reported screening conditions summarized for Kaur et al. (2024): 0.03 M ketoacid, 5 equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, and 72 h. Use an anoxic, sulfide-free batch with an accessible metallic catalyst surface. This models cool hydrogen-bearing aqueous pores or a laboratory analogue, not a 350-600 K vent interior. The low-ammonia alanine result is not assigned to leucine.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible carbonyl-ammonia condensation forms an imine/iminium intermediate, and nickel activates hydrogen for reduction to leucine. Direct carbonyl hydrogenation competes through rxn_015.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly demonstrated leucine formation from alpha-ketoisocaproate with hydrogen and nickel-containing catalysts, with no reaction in metal-free controls. The reported 6-84% product-yield range spans several substrates and is not a leucine-specific yield. The supported nickel formulation is a laboratory implementation; native nickel is a geological candidate, not an assumed equivalent catalyst. The upstream ketoacid source remains unresolved. Sulfide passivation is avoided by declaring an independent sulfide-free branch rather than assuming transport from the photochemical network.

reactions.name: Iron-meteorite-catalyzed reductive amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate
agents: Ground Aletai iron meteorite with accessible Fe-Ni metallic surfaces

conditions.catalyst: Ground Aletai iron meteorite, reported loading corresponding to 18 mol% Ni
conditions.other: Use the reported screening framework: 0.03 M ketoacid, 5 equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, and 72 h. Maintain anoxia and exclude sulfide carryover. Catalyst activity requires exposed metal; particle size, weathering state and surface oxidation must be characterized rather than inferred from bulk meteorite composition.

reactions.mechanism: Accessible meteoritic metallic surfaces activate hydrogen and reduce the ketoacid-derived imine/iminium pool to leucine; carbonyl reduction can also generate the hydroxy acid.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated reductive amination of the leucine ketoacid using ground iron meteorite. This supports a distinct catalyst implementation, not an independent solution to carbon-skeleton formation. Meteorite delivery establishes a possible metal source but does not guarantee that weathered or sulfide-exposed particles remain active. No leucine-specific yield is inferred from the aggregate substrate range.

reactions.name: Palladium-catalyzed reductive amination benchmark

conditions.other: Reported screening framework: 0.03 M ketoacid, 5 equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, and 72 h. Use an anoxic, sulfide-free aqueous batch. This is primarily an experimental catalytic benchmark; a natural Pd/C material or adequate exposed geological palladium concentration is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Palladium activates molecular hydrogen for reduction of the ketoacid-derived imine/iminium intermediate, favoring amino-acid formation over direct carbonyl reduction in the reported substrate screen.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated leucine formation with palladium catalysis. The 52-88% yields and greater-than-5:1 amino-acid/hydroxy-acid selectivity summarize multiple substrates and must not be assigned specifically to leucine. Palladium's rarity and sulfur sensitivity weaken geological generality despite strong laboratory evidence. This route still depends on supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate.

reactions.name: Competing nickel-catalyzed reduction to alpha-hydroxyisocaproate

conditions.other: Competing channel under the same batch conditions as rxn_012: 0.03 M initial ketoacid, pH 8, 5 equivalents NH4HCO3 in the surrounding mixture, and 72 h. Ammonia is not consumed in this particular net channel. Quantify hydroxy acid together with leucine rather than treating ketoacid disappearance as amination yield.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogenation of the ketoacid carbonyl produces 2-hydroxy-4-methylpentanoic acid without nitrogen incorporation.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) reported competing hydroxy-acid formation with nickel and meteorite catalysts, with approximately comparable amino- and hydroxy-acid amounts across the reported substrate set. This is a chemically required selectivity limitation, not an additional route to leucine. No exact leucine-specific branching ratio is claimed, and no unverified hydroxy-acid recycling reaction is added.

pathways.name: Methane-fed discharge endpoint
pathways.description: Experimentally supported leucine endpoint from a methane-containing discharge and aqueous collection system. The reaction node includes an explicitly distinguished analytical completion benchmark; it does not establish selective free-leucine accumulation in an unprocessed natural pool.

pathways.name: Isobutane-fed discharge endpoint
pathways.description: Experimentally supported alternative hydrocarbon feed. This is an operational feedstock variant of mixed discharge chemistry, not an independently resolved leucine-specific mechanism.

pathways.name: Acetylene-fed discharge endpoint
pathways.description: Experimentally supported unsaturated-carbon feed yielding leucine among a complex product mixture. The relatively favorable glycine-normalized abundance does not imply high absolute yield or biological-isomer selectivity.

pathways.name: H2S-rich volcanic discharge endpoint
pathways.description: Empirical route corresponding to the leucine-containing archived H2S discharge experiment. Radical enhancement is a mechanistic interpretation; the formal sulfur sink and analytical hydrolysis are not presented as a measured natural sequence.

pathways.name: Acetone homologation followed by benchmark aminonitrile hydrolysis
pathways.description: Acetone enters two staged reductive homologations, followed by ammonia conversion to the leucine aminonitrile. Literature support reaches the aminonitrile. The final forcing hydrolysis is an explicitly identified extension requiring leucine-specific recovery and crude-mixture compatibility measurements; a complete natural acetone-to-leucine sequence is not established.

pathways.name: Direct isovaleraldehyde Strecker route
pathways.description: Supplied 3-methylbutanal reacts with ammonia and cyanide to give the correctly connected leucine aminonitrile, followed by forcing acid hydrolysis. The aldehyde inventory is declared rather than assigned an unverified selective origin. Naturally achievable hydrolysis rates remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Isovaleraldehyde cyanohydrin-first Strecker variant
pathways.description: Supplied aldehyde first accumulates as its cyanohydrin, then enters ammonia-mediated aminonitrile formation and forcing hydrolysis. This differs in reagent sequencing from P6 but shares Strecker chemistry and the same hydrolysis bottleneck; it is not an independent validation of that bottleneck.

pathways.name: Supplied ketoacid with supported nickel and hydrogen
pathways.description: Experimentally demonstrated terminal amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate. The competing hydroxy-acid channel is rxn_015 and is not counted as a target-producing step. Neither ketoacid synthesis nor equivalence between supported laboratory nickel and native geological nickel is assumed.

pathways.name: Supplied ketoacid with meteoritic Fe-Ni and hydrogen
pathways.description: Experimentally demonstrated terminal amination using ground iron meteorite. The branch requires an accessible, unpassivated metallic surface and a supplied ketoacid inventory; no transfer from a sulfidic reactor is assumed.

pathways.name: Supplied ketoacid with palladium and hydrogen
pathways.description: Experimentally supported catalytic benchmark for terminal leucine synthesis. Palladium availability and catalyst formulation limit geological interpretation, and this pathway does not resolve the origin of alpha-ketoisocaproate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring et al. (1972) and Ring & Miller (1984), as summarized in the supplied research, support leucine production in methane-fed discharge experiments. The reaction is acceptable as an explicitly empirical formation-and-workup module, not an elementary mechanism. Its inferred balance does not establish actual hydrogen yield. Surface discharge is appropriate, but the submitted record does not specify the experimental conditions or physically justify a natural equivalent of the analytical hydrolysis.
suggestions: Attach the experimental gas composition, nitrogen sources, aqueous conditions, discharge duration and workup protocol to rxn_001.
Distinguish leucine measured after hydrolysis from free leucine present before workup; report the cited Leu/Gly ratio rather than implying selective conversion.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Ring & Miller (1984) findings support an isobutane-fed discharge endpoint containing leucine, with approximately 6.7 leucine molecules per 100 glycine molecules. This is an observed product channel, not evidence for the displayed equation as a selective overall conversion. The declared feedstock inventory is accepted; its geological supply is a separate question. Environmental confidence is limited mainly by missing formation and workup conditions.
suggestions: Link rxn_002 to the specific experimental run and record its complete gas mixture, discharge conditions and analytical workup.
Preserve the distinction between the observed leucine endpoint and the unmeasured hydrogen stoichiometry of the formal channel.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring & Miller (1984) support leucine detection in the acetylene-fed experiment. The reported value of 14 leucine molecules per 100 glycine molecules is a relative abundance, not a 14% feedstock yield. The authoritative balance check validates conservation, and omitting other discharge products is acceptable for the declared empirical product-channel representation. The missing experimental recipe and hydrolysis details prevent stronger environmental assessment.
suggestions: Provide the acetylene experiment's actual reaction and workup conditions with its primary citation.
Annotate the equation as a formal leucine channel that cannot predict total conversion, selectivity or the complete product mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Parker et al. (2011) provide direct support for leucine in the analyzed products of Miller's H2S-rich discharge experiment. A locally reducing volcanic setting is a plausible formation context, although natural implementation of the complete formation-and-workup sequence is not established. The formal S8 sink and inferred hydrogen coefficients satisfy conservation but are not experimentally established coproduct distributions. The network appropriately avoids claiming a complete discharge mechanism.
suggestions: Record the reported gas partial pressures, boiling-water arrangement, three-day discharge and subsequent analytical processing.
Retain sulfur-product uncertainty and distinguish the experimentally analyzed endpoint from free leucine production in an untreated natural pool.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Patel et al. (2015) support the staged acetone-derived route to the leucine aminonitrile, not the completed leucine sequence represented here. The carbon-skeleton progression is correct, and all net transformations conserve atoms and charge. Conventional acid hydrolysis provides a credible chemical completion. However, the submitted network does not actually specify the claimed hydrolysis benchmark's acid, concentration, temperature or duration, nor the detailed photochemical staging and transition into hydrolysis.
suggestions: Document the reduction/deoxygenation and recyanation operations within each homologation module, including UV exposure, sulfide and cyanide dosing, pH, and any required copper catalyst.
Provide a referenced, substrate-appropriate acid-hydrolysis protocol and explain acidification, heating or physical transfer from the surface photochemical setting.
Measure cumulative aminonitrile and leucine yields through the staged sequence without treating the formal S8 sink as a measured sulfur-product distribution.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Isovaleraldehyde is the correct aldehyde for a leucine Strecker synthesis, and the aminonitrile followed by hydrolysis gives the correct racemic target. Accepting isovaleraldehyde as a declared starting inventory does not introduce a missing reaction. The principal unresolved issue is operational and environmental: ammonia/HCN speciation and the forcing hydrolysis conditions are unspecified, and the Surface-to-Biochemical labels do not explain how the required change in conditions occurs.
suggestions: Specify aldehyde, ammonia and HCN concentrations, pH and reaction time to assess competition with cyanohydrin formation.
Document the hydrolysis benchmark and distinguish its laboratory validity from any proposed naturally occurring acidification and heating process.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyanohydrin-first route has the correct carbon skeleton and is consistent with cyanohydrin/aldehyde equilibria followed by imine and aminonitrile formation. rxn_008 should be understood as a net equilibrium-mediated conversion, not necessarily direct hydroxyl displacement by ammonia. The route can chemically reach racemic leucine, but its completion depends on the same incompletely specified acid-hydrolysis benchmark as P5 and P6.
suggestions: Describe the equilibrium-mediated mechanism and specify ammonia loading, pH and residence time for rxn_008.
Monitor competing cyanohydrin hydrolysis to hydroxy acids and supply the final aminonitrile-hydrolysis protocol.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly support nickel-catalyzed conversion of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate to leucine. The supplied research reports reference conditions of 22 °C, pH 8 and 5 bar H2, but these are absent from the reaction record. rxn_015 is evaluated here as the associated competing reduction, not an additional leucine-forming step. Its inclusion appropriately acknowledges selectivity loss. The unspecified Biochemical environment does not establish availability of the experimental supported catalyst.
suggestions: Specify catalyst support and loading, ammonium source and concentration, hydrogen pressure, temperature and reaction duration.
Add leucine-specific conversion and amino-acid/hydroxy-acid selectivity; do not substitute the seven-substrate yield range or low-ammonia alanine results.
Separate demonstrated supported-nickel catalysis from any proposed naturally occurring catalyst analogue.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Kaur et al. (2024) findings directly support leucine formation using ground Aletai iron meteorite, ammonia and hydrogen. This provides an experimentally tested natural catalyst material, although the required exposure, loading and hydrogen conditions are not established for the network's unspecified environment. The route is strong conditional on its declared ketoacid inventory; it does not demonstrate that inventory's abiotic synthesis. Hydroxy-acid competition should also be represented for this catalyst.
suggestions: Record meteorite composition, accessible metallic surface, particle size or preparation, catalyst loading and the complete hydrogen/ammonium protocol.
Annotate or add the meteorite-catalyzed hydroxy-acid branch and obtain leucine-specific yield and selectivity data.
If making a natural-setting claim, justify co-location of the declared inventory, active meteoritic surfaces and sustained hydrogen availability.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) support palladium-catalyzed reductive amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate. This is a strong laboratory benchmark and a chemically valid target-producing step. Its explicit benchmark status appropriately avoids asserting a demonstrated natural implementation. Environmental confidence remains lower because the Biochemical label provides neither the hydrogenation conditions nor evidence for an equivalent accessible Pd catalyst. The reported multi-substrate selectivity range should not be presented as a leucine-specific measurement.
suggestions: Specify the experimentally used Pd catalyst, support, loading and full reaction conditions, with a direct citation.
Keep laboratory benchmark performance separate from natural applicability and report leucine-specific analytical results.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid: all 19 molecule nodes and 15 reaction nodes are connected, molecule IDs are consistent, and the authoritative balance check reports no atom or charge conservation violations. The larger inferred coefficients are compatible with the declared lumped channels and S8 bookkeeping; they do not independently establish mechanisms or measured coproduct yields. Terminal sulfur and hydroxy-acid nodes are legitimate connected products, not isolated or broken pathways. Chemically, the network has strong support for discharge/workup endpoints, the cyanosulfidic aminonitrile sequence, conventional Strecker chemistry and supplied-ketoacid reductive amination. Its explicit separation of experimentally observed products, precursor-only demonstrations and laboratory benchmarks is appropriate. Declaring alpha-ketoisocaproate as a starting inventory makes P8-P10 valid conditional routes; its unresolved origin limits prebiotic self-sufficiency rather than invalidating those reactions. No transfer of sulfidic material into the metal-catalyzed branches is required or assumed. The main shortcomings are missing reaction-level protocols and citations, incompletely specified hydrolysis, and insufficient physical justification for the stated environmental transitions and catalyst settings. Surface and Biochemical labels alone cannot establish these conditions. The supplied literature supports racemic leucine production but not a demonstrated naturally operating implementation of every complete route. Low yield and poor isomer selectivity are limitations, not failures to produce the target. No score bonus is assigned for ten route labels, shared molecules or convergence. Overall confidence is below the 0.90 network approval threshold, so the network is not approved at that threshold; the pathway approval flags use the separately requested 0.80 threshold.
